messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The first time it happened, Carlos was thirty-one, a junior accountant still living in the old neighborhood in East Los Angeles. He had stayed late at his desk, finishing a client’s quarterly returns, and was walking to his car when two officers pulled up. They were looking for someone else—a man who matched nothing about Carlos except the color of his skin and the fact that he was walking alone after dark. Carlos did not understand what was happening until he was on the ground, his cheek pressed against the asphalt, a knee grinding into his lower back, and a voice shouting words he could not process. He did not resist. He did not speak. He lay still and waited for it to stop, and when it did, he was left with a cracked rib, a split lip, and a quiet, persistent sense that something in the world had shifted permanently out of alignment. No charges were filed. No apology came. The department’s internal review found no wrongdoing, and Carlos was left to go back to his life.

But the life he returned to was not the same. In the weeks that followed, he noticed that he could not stop thinking about the other people he had seen in similar moments—the man on the news whose hands were cuffed behind his back, the woman whose brother had been pulled over and never came home. These were not his memories, but they arrived in his mind with the same force as his own, and he could not separate them. He began to avoid news reports, then television altogether. He stopped visiting parts of the city he had known since childhood because he could not tell which streets were safe and which were not. He had always been a methodical person, someone who liked to plan, but now that planning took on a new shape. Before entering any building, he scanned the room for exits, noted the layout of the corridors, and chose a seat that gave him a clear line of sight to the door. He could not relax unless he knew exactly how he would leave. At home, he found himself checking the locks repeatedly, and when he walked to his car, he glanced over his shoulder every few steps, certain that someone was behind him even when no one was there.

The divorce came five years later, though Carlos could not say for certain whether the marriage ended because of what had happened or whether it would have ended anyway. His wife had told him that he was not present, that he had become distant and irritable, that he did not want to go anywhere or do anything. She was right. He had stopped wanting to be around people because being around people meant being seen, and being seen felt dangerous. He had come to believe that there was something about him—something in his face, his posture, the way he moved through the world—that had made the officers stop that night. He did not know what it was, but he was certain it was there, and he was certain that others could see it too. This belief made him withdraw further. He worked from home when he could, and when he had to meet clients in person, he kept the meetings short and neutral. He did not tell anyone at the firm what had happened. He did not tell anyone anything.

Now, at fifty-three, Carlos lives alone in a small apartment in a suburb he chose specifically because the streets are quiet and the parking lot is well lit. He still works as a tax consultant, but his caseload has shrunk. He cannot take on new clients who want to meet in unfamiliar offices, and he has turned down several opportunities that would have required him to travel to parts of the city he does not know. His body has begun to ache in ways it did not before—a persistent pain in his lower back, where the knee had pressed him into the ground—and each time he feels it, he is pulled back into that night. The pain is not just physical. It is a reminder that the event is not over, that it lives inside him and will not leave.

What finally brought Carlos to seek help was a morning in late October when he woke up and realized he could not remember the last time he had felt anything other than tired. He had been thinking, more often than he wanted to admit, that he was not sure his life was worth living anymore. He did not have a plan. He did not even have a clear wish. But the thought had settled into him like a low hum, and it would not stop. He made the appointment because he did not know what else to do, and because a part of him—a part he had almost forgotten—still wanted to believe that there might be a way out of this. He is afraid that the therapist will not understand, that she will see the same thing in him that he has always seen in himself. But he is also afraid of what will happen if he does not try.
